practices.name: Topical minoxidil
practices.claim: Minoxidil applied to the scalp thickens thinning hair and regrows lost hair in male pattern baldness.
practices.evidence_rationale: It is sold without a prescription with FDA-labeled use to regrow hair on the top of the scalp in men, and meta-analyses of placebo-controlled trials find more hair growth than placebo. Only a subset of users get cosmetically meaningful regrowth, and gains last only while it is used.
practices.risk_rationale: Common effects are scalp irritation and unwanted facial hair, and the label tells users to stop for chest pain, rapid heartbeat, dizziness or sudden swelling. One case report describes low blood pressure after far too much was applied, so overuse is the main avoidable problem.
key_harms: chest pain, rapid heartbeat or dizziness (stop-use signs)
hair loss resumes if you stop

legal_status.US: Non-prescription (OTC): FDA Drug Facts labeling covers regrowing hair on the top of the scalp in men.
legal_status.AU: Pharmacy medicine (Schedule 2), available without a prescription.
legal_status.CA: Listed as a non-prescription drug in Health Canada's Drug Product Database.

practices.name: Low-dose oral minoxidil
practices.claim: A low-dose minoxidil tablet regrows hair across the scalp as well as or better than the topical solution, without having to apply a solution to the scalp.
practices.evidence_rationale: Four randomized trials (279 patients) found oral minoxidil no different from the topical on hair density or diameter over about 6 to 9 months, and the topical has placebo-controlled proof. The trials compared oral with topical rather than with placebo, the FDA does not list hair loss as an approved use, and nothing shows it beats the topical.
practices.risk_rationale: The FDA label for minoxidil tablets opens with a warning about fluid around the heart and worsened angina in its approved hypertension use; in hair-loss use, reviews report mostly excess hair growth, swelling and dizziness, and fluid around the heart is extremely rare and often tied to compounding errors. It needs a prescriber who checks blood pressure, heart history and other medicines, which self-sourcing skips.
key_harms: unwanted face and body hair, about twice as often as with the topical
dizziness, low blood pressure or fast heartbeat
practices.safer_alternative: Start with a licensed topical, or ask a dermatologist or GP about prescription options; if the oral route is on the table, they check blood pressure, heart history and other medicines first and follow up.

legal_status.US: Off-label. Minoxidil tablets are prescription-only and labeled for severe hypertension; the FDA label says use to promote hair growth is not an approved indication.
legal_status.AU: Prescription-only (Schedule 4); the listed tablet product is registered for severe refractory hypertension.
legal_status.CA: Prescription-only in Health Canada's Drug Product Database; the listed tablet product is classed as an antihypertensive.

practices.name: Finasteride
practices.claim: Finasteride stops male pattern balding in nearly all men and regrows noticeable hair in most.
practices.evidence_rationale: It is FDA-approved for male pattern hair loss in men on the strength of three double-blind placebo-controlled trials (1,879 men), and a meta-analysis of randomized trials confirms it beats placebo. In the label's five-year vertex data about 9 in 10 men had no further visible loss, but only about half showed visible regrowth.
practices.risk_rationale: The FDA label and the MHRA both list depression, suicidal thoughts and sexual dysfunction that can continue after stopping, and the MHRA notes the hair-loss strength is commonly prescribed online, where these risks may not be explained. Most men tolerate it and causation of the psychiatric reports is still debated, but the harms that do occur can be long-lasting.
key_harms: lower sex drive, erection or ejaculation problems
sexual side effects that can persist after stopping
possible rise in high-grade prostate cancer detection
practices.safer_alternative: Use a prescriber who asks about depression history, explains the sexual and mood risks up front, and agrees a plan to stop and report symptoms; a licensed topical minoxidil is a non-hormonal option to try first.

legal_status.US: Prescription-only; FDA-approved for male pattern hair loss in men.
legal_status.UK: Prescription-only; approved for male pattern hair loss. The hair-loss strength is available only on private prescription and is commonly prescribed online (MHRA).
legal_status.CA: Prescription drug; marketed in Canada for male pattern hair loss since 1998.

practices.name: Scalp microneedling
practices.claim: Rolling or stamping a microneedle device over the scalp regrows thinning hair and makes minoxidil work much better.
practices.evidence_rationale: Three meta-analyses of 10 to 13 small randomized trials find more hair growth when microneedling is added to minoxidil than with minoxidil alone, but results vary widely between trials and a network meta-analysis ranks microneedling alone below oral 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors such as finasteride. The FDA's list of authorized microneedling uses does not include hair loss.
practices.risk_rationale: Most side effects are short-lived redness, bleeding and crusting, but the FDA warns that some can be permanent, that reusing a needle cartridge is unsafe, and that these devices are not approved for pushing topical drugs into the skin. The FDA page does not discuss home use, where sterility and technique are left to the user.
key_harms: risks of combining with topical drugs are unknown (FDA)
practices.safer_alternative: If you want to try it, a trained provider using a new single-use needle cartridge is the route the FDA describes.

legal_status.US: The FDA has authorized microneedling devices for facial acne scars, facial wrinkles and abdominal scars in adults 22 and older; hair loss is not among the authorized uses listed.

sources.supports: evidence_rationale: 13 randomized trials (696 patients) favored combined microneedling over single treatments for hair density and diameter.

practices.name: Resistance training
practices.claim: Lifting weights builds muscle and lowers body fat, giving a visibly better physique.
practices.evidence_rationale: A meta-analysis of 111 studies found about 1.5 kg of added muscle mass in healthy men, and a meta-analysis of randomized trials found resistance training lowers body fat percentage and fat mass in healthy adults, though the fat loss on its own is modest. US public-health guidance includes muscle-strengthening activity for adults.
practices.risk_rationale: Reviews of competitive weight-training sports find low injury rates, mostly strains and tendinitis of the shoulder, lower back and knee. Most of that data comes from competitive athletes, so rates in casual lifters are less certain.

sources.title: A Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis of the Effect of Resistance Training on Whole-Body Muscle Growth in Healthy Adult Males
sources.publisher: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
sources.supports: evidence_rationale: 111 studies (1,927 men) showed a pooled muscle mass gain of about 1.5 kg with no heterogeneity across studies.

sources.title: The Effect of Resistance Training in Healthy Adults on Body Fat Percentage, Fat Mass and Visceral Fat: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
sources.supports: evidence_rationale: in randomized trials versus control (the review has 58 studies, 54 in the meta-analysis), resistance training reduced body fat percentage, fat mass and visceral fat.

sources.title: Adult Activity: An Overview
sources.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.supports: evidence_rationale: US public-health guidance for adults includes muscle-strengthening activity across all major muscle groups.

sources.title: The Epidemiology of Injuries Across the Weight-Training Sports
sources.supports: risk_rationale and key_harms: low injury rates relative to common team sports; shoulder, lower back, knee, elbow and wrist most affected; strains, tendinitis and sprains most common; most studies retrospective and of competitive athletes.

practices.name: Consistent sleep (7+ hours)
practices.claim: Getting consistent sleep of 7 or more hours a night makes your skin, eyes and face look healthier and more attractive.
practices.evidence_rationale: One lab experiment found sleep-deprived faces were rated less healthy and less attractive, a second found more visible fatigue cues such as darker eye circles and paler skin, and a comparison of 60 women links poor sleep quality with worse skin-ageing and skin-barrier recovery measures. The samples are small, the experiments test total sleep deprivation (31 hours awake) rather than 7 or more hours versus slightly less, and the visible effects were small.
practices.risk_rationale: Getting enough sleep carries no meaningful harm. Ongoing trouble sleeping is a reason to see a doctor, not to self-medicate.

sources.title: Beauty sleep: experimental study on the perceived health and attractiveness of sleep deprived people
sources.supports: evidence_rationale: 23 adults photographed after normal sleep and after sleep deprivation were rated by 65 observers as less healthy, more tired and less attractive when sleep deprived (small differences).

sources.title: Cues of fatigue: effects of sleep deprivation on facial appearance
sources.supports: evidence_rationale: faces after sleep deprivation were rated as having darker eye circles, paler skin and more wrinkles and fine lines.

sources.title: Does poor sleep quality affect skin ageing?
sources.supports: evidence_rationale: in 60 women, good sleepers had lower intrinsic skin-ageing scores, better barrier recovery and better self-rated appearance than poor sleepers.

sources.title: Recommended Amount of Sleep for a Healthy Adult: A Joint Consensus Statement of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine and Sleep Research Society
sources.supports: claim and practice name: professional-body consensus that adults need 7 or more hours of sleep per night for optimal health. Says nothing about appearance or skin.

sources.title: About Sleep
sources.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.supports: claim and practice name (adults 18-60 need 7 or more hours); risk_rationale sentence 2 (talk to a healthcare provider about problems sleeping). Says nothing about appearance or skin.

proposed.name: Dutasteride for hair loss (off-label)
proposed.why: A 2024 network meta-analysis ranked it highest for hair density among monotherapies, and in May 2026 the MHRA announced a precautionary mood-alteration warning for its product information, so it deserves its own evidence and risk grade.
